title: When GRACE Measures More Than Water: Geomorphic Mass Redistribution in Terrestrial Water Storage Trends
content:
Abstract

The Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment and its Follow-On missions (GRACE/GRACE-FO) provide indirect estimates of regional-scale water storage changes, albeit at a coarse resolution (∼300 km). Interpreting GRACE-derived trends in geomorphically complex settings presents additional challenges. High rates of soil erosion, sediment transport, and deposition can affect gravity signals when they produce net mass export, accumulation, or source-sink redistribution at GRACE-relevant scales. Geomorphic correction of the GRACE signal is meaningful in arid regions, where sediment dynamics are active and terrestrial water storage variation is dominated by groundwater overdraft. In temperate and tropical climates, geomorphic mass redistribution becomes negligible as terrestrial water storage changes are much larger. Downscaled GRACE-FO products may misrepresent groundwater storage changes if they are not grounded in a robust hydrogeological conceptualization. In this commentary, we discuss how sediment dynamics may affect hydrological GRACE-based assessments using examples from arid source-to-sink sediment corridors. These cases illustrate that sediment transport models and hydrogeological conceptual models are essential tools for improving the interpretation of GRACE-derived trends in hyper-arid climates and catchments with accelerated erosion.
